title: Pollo al Mattone
subtitle: Tuscan spatchcocked chicken pressed flat and grilled with lemon and rosemary
excerpt: Pollo al mattone -- chicken under a brick -- is a Tuscan technique for cooking a whole spatchcocked chicken under a heavy weight that presses it flat against a hot pan or grill. The weight speeds up cooking, gives even contact with the heat source, and produces the crispiest possible skin. The marinade of lemon, garlic, rosemary, and olive oil is classic Tuscan.
sourceNotes: Pollo al mattone (chicken under a brick) is a Florentine and Tuscan grilling technique, making use of a heavy stone or brick to press a spatchcocked chicken flat during cooking. The technique appears in Pellegrino Artusi's La Scienza in Cucina (1891) and is widely considered the definitive Tuscan way of cooking a whole chicken. Traditionally done on an outdoor grill over charcoal, it works equally well in a cast-iron pan.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Marinate the spatchcocked chicken for up to 4 hours before cooking.
recipe.temperatureNote: Cook on the hob in a cast-iron pan, or on an outdoor grill over direct heat.

content.text: To spatchcock a chicken, place it breast-side down and cut out the backbone with kitchen scissors. Then flip it over and press hard on the breastbone to flatten. The mattone (brick) can be any heavy weight: a wrapped brick, a heavy cast-iron pan, or a pot filled with water. The weight is placed on the chicken as soon as it goes into the pan, and stays there for the first 20 minutes of cooking.

items.prepNote: juice of both, zest of one

content.text: Mix {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} oil, {{lemon}} lemon juice and zest, {{garlic}} garlic, {{rosemary}} rosemary, {{chilli-flakes}} chilli flakes (if using), {{salt-flakes}} salt, and {{black-pepper}} pepper together. Rub this mixture all over the {{whole-chicken}} spatchcocked chicken, getting under the breast skin. Leave to marinate for at least 1 hour, or up to 4 hours.

Heat a large cast-iron pan over medium-high heat. Place the chicken skin-side down. Put a second heavy pan or wrapped brick on top of the chicken to press it flat. Cook for 20 minutes without moving the chicken, keeping it pressed down.

Remove the weight. Flip the chicken onto the bone side. Replace the weight. Cook for a further 20 to 25 minutes until the chicken is cooked through -- the juices must run clear at the thigh joint and the internal temperature at the thickest part of the thigh must read 74C. Rest the chicken for 10 minutes before cutting into pieces.

items.symptom: The skin is pale after 20 minutes skin-side down
items.cause: The pan was not hot enough before the chicken went in.
items.fix: The pan must be fully hot before the chicken is placed in it. If the skin is pale at 20 minutes, remove the weight, increase the heat, and cook for a further 5 minutes before flipping.

content.text: Pollo al mattone is associated with Florence and Tuscany, but the technique of weighting a flattened bird during cooking is ancient and appears in Roman cooking literature. In Tuscany it is made on the grill (grigliate) over wood or charcoal in summer. The brick or stone is purely functional: it creates total contact between the skin and the heat source, giving the fastest possible crispness without drying the meat. Pellegrino Artusi described the technique in 1891 as a Florentine standard.
